extracted.intended_audience: machine learning researchers, conference reviewers, and academic hiring/hiring-committee members
extracted.subtask_description: Opinionated guidance and evaluative principles about how peer review currently functions in machine learning conferences and how reviewers and the community should behave and reform practices. Focuses on scalability, what peer review fails to accomplish, and norms for reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to elevate great work
rubrics_metrics.description: "It doesn't elevate great work" — peer review fails to reliably surface the best research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a criterion when judging the effectiveness of peer review: ask whether the process actually lifts outstanding work. The author argues defenders cannot articulate what peer review accomplishes well or that it is superior to alternatives, implying that elevation of great work is not a demonstrated strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error detection
rubrics_metrics.description: "It doesn't catch errors" — peer review is not effective at finding methodological or factual mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given high submission volumes and limited reviewer time, expecting comprehensive error detection is unrealistic. Treat peer review as a coarse filter rather than a mechanism that will reliably catch errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraud detection
rubrics_metrics.description: "It doesn't catch fraud" — peer review is poor at identifying fraudulent or deliberately deceptive work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on peer review as a primary mechanism for fraud prevention; structural vulnerabilities (including collusion) and scale constraints limit its effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance to manipulation / collusion
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate review processes for their vulnerability to organized manipulation. The existence of collusion rings undermines trust in peer review outcomes and should be considered when designing or assessing reviewing systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scalability of meaningful evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Capacity to provide meaningful evaluation at scale — the author notes ICML / NeurIPS receive ~30,000 submissions annually and reviewers have about six weeks to review six or more papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use submission volume and reviewer time as metrics to judge whether a reviewing model can produce substantive, high-quality assessments. The page argues that, at current scales, meaningful evaluation is impossible, so any rubric must factor in realistic resource constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid adding unfunded requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: "Adding requirements without resources creates worse outcomes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing new mandatory procedures (e.g., ethics statements, preregistration plans, extra paperwork), assess whether venues provide the resources to implement and enforce them. The author warns such mandates without funding will strangle creativity and can enable authoritarian control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer role expectation: quick filter not oracle
rubrics_metrics.description: A reviewer should "resist treating their own review as a definitive certification — it is a quick filter at scale, not an oracle."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt reviewer norms that recognize practical limits: perform lightweight triage/filtering rather than exhaustive certification. Avoid asking authors to perform additional work that the venue will not fund or support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer organic cultural reform over mandates
rubrics_metrics.description: "Devalue peer-reviewed papers through cultural shift, not new rules."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider incentive- and culture-focused reforms (e.g., hiring committees de-emphasizing publication counts) rather than top-down rule changes. The author notes hiring committees already distrust candidates with excessive publication counts, suggesting cultural levers can reduce perverse incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware social-media-as-alternative conflation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Social media bypasses peer review but conflates scientific debate, public communication, and personal opinion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using social media or single-platform alternatives to peer review, explicitly separate modes of communication. The author endorses Kevin Munger's critique that single-platform conflation is problematic; treat public discussion, scientific debate, and personal views as distinct activities.
